materials.title: Mole’s window
materials.text:
In this imaginary story, Mole wants a window for his little underground room. Fox offers to draw one on the wall. He paints blue sky, a yellow sun and a bird with a very long tail. Mole likes the picture, but the room is still dark when he closes his lamp.

"Your window does not let in light," Mole says. Fox agrees. It is a picture of a window, not a real opening. They ask Badger to help them find a better place for a workroom. Badger shows them a small room near the surface, with daylight coming through a real window.

Mole moves his drawing table there. He keeps his old room for sleeping and asks Fox to paint another picture on its wall. This time, he does not expect it to light the room. A picture can be lovely without doing the work of the thing it shows. Fox paints a night sky, and Mole puts his lamp beside the bed.

questions.prompt: What does Mole want at first?
options: A window for his underground room
questions.explanation: Opening states window request. Tail belongs drawing and bird not purchase request.

questions.prompt: Why does the painted window not solve the problem?
options: It does not let daylight into the room
The painted bird closes the window
Fox uses too much yellow for real sunlight
questions.explanation: Painting is representation, not opening. Pigment amount/bird action not physical cause.

questions.prompt: Who helps find another room?
questions.explanation: Badger shows surface room. Bird imaginary drawing/teacher absent.

questions.prompt: What is the old room used for later?
questions.explanation: Mole keeps old room for sleep. Other uses unstated.

questions.prompt: Why can Mole enjoy the second painting?
options: It removes the need for any lamp
He no longer expects it to act as a real window
questions.explanation: He separates picture pleasure from function. Sunlight/no lamp claims contradict night painting and lamp.

materials.title: The drumstick in the garden
materials.text:
Nina practises her small drum in the garden. One drumstick rolls under a bush. She looks for it but finds only a dry branch. The branch is about the same length, so she tries it on the drum. It makes a sound, but its rough end catches on the surface.

Nina stops and calls her uncle. He asks her to leave the branch aside while they search together. They lift the low leaves carefully and find the drumstick beside a stone. Nina is pleased, but she asks why the branch did not work well when it looked so similar.

Her uncle shows her the smooth, rounded end of the drumstick. Its shape matters, not only its length. Nina puts both proper sticks into their bag before going inside. She keeps the branch for a nature drawing, where its rough edges are useful details to notice. It was the wrong tool for her drum, but it was not useless for everything.

questions.prompt: Where does the drumstick roll?
questions.explanation: It rolls under bush. River/cupboard absent.

questions.prompt: Why does Nina first try the branch?
options: It is about the same length
Her uncle says it is perfect
It has been made for her drum
questions.explanation: Similar length prompts trial. Special manufacture/uncle approval not given.

questions.prompt: What makes Nina stop?
options: The bush begins to move away
The rough end catches on the drum surface
questions.explanation: Rough branch catches; other events invented.

questions.prompt: What detail does her uncle point out?
options: Length is the only useful feature
Every branch is the same as every drumstick
The proper drumstick has a smooth rounded end
questions.explanation: He contrasts end shape. Universal equality/length-only contradict explanation.

questions.prompt: What happens to the branch?
options: Nina uses it as a subject for a nature drawing
It is put into the drum’s musical score
questions.explanation: Kept for observational drawing. It is not used again to strike or inserted as score.

materials.title: Four holiday postcards
materials.text:
Four postcards arrived at the class display. These are fictional messages.

A. Leo — Lake Town, Tuesday. I am staying with my aunt for five days. We went out in a boat this morning. Tomorrow, if the weather is good, we will walk around the lake. I have drawn the boat on the front.

B. Maya — Hill Village, Wednesday. We arrived by train yesterday. Our family is staying for a week. The small museum opens only in the afternoon, so we will visit after lunch. I chose a postcard showing the old bridge.

C. Sam — Coast City, Friday. We came by coach on Monday and will leave on Sunday. The beach is windy today. Yesterday we visited an aquarium. My postcard has a picture of a sea turtle.

D. Asha — River Farm, Sunday. I am here with my grandparents for the weekend. We fed the hens before breakfast and picked apples later. We will return home this evening. The picture on my card shows the red barn.

questions.prompt: Who is staying with an aunt?
questions.explanation: A Leo stays aunt5days. Maya family/Sam coach trip not aunt.

questions.prompt: When did Maya arrive in Hill Village?
questions.explanation: Wednesday message says yesterday, Tuesday. Wednesday writing and Friday Sam date.

questions.prompt: Which place did Sam visit on Thursday?
questions.explanation: Friday card says aquarium yesterday, Thursday. Farm Asha/bridge Maya picture.

questions.prompt: Which card shows a building used on a farm?
questions.explanation: Asha red barn. Leo boat, Sam turtle.

questions.prompt: Who plans to go home on the day the card is written?
questions.explanation: Sunday Asha returns this evening. Leo5days/Mayaweek not same-day departure.

materials.title: Four club taster sessions
materials.text:
The school offers four fictional taster sessions next Saturday. Each booking is for one session. Leave at least thirty minutes between sessions to move rooms and get ready. A parent books a place in advance.

A. Paper Boats — 09:00–10:00, Art Room. Ages9–12. Cost£4. All paper is provided. Bring a box to carry the boat home.

B. Junior Choir — 10:15–11:15, Music Room. Ages10–13. Free. No singing experience is needed. Bring water. No instrument is required.

C. Story Pictures — 10:45–12:00, Library. Ages8–11. Cost£3. Draw one scene from a story. Bring your favourite short book; pencils and paper are supplied.

D. Garden Watch — 13:00–14:00, Garden Room. Ages11–14. Cost£2. Observe garden wildlife with a teacher. Wear shoes suitable for outdoor paths. The meeting room is indoors, but part of the session is outside.

questions.prompt: Which session is free?
questions.explanation: B costs nothing. A£4,D£2.

questions.prompt: What does a Paper Boats participant bring?
questions.explanation: Box required; paper supplied, instrument irrelevant.

questions.prompt: Which session can an eight-year-old attend?
questions.explanation: C8–11 includes8. B starts10,D11.

questions.prompt: Can a ten-year-old book Paper Boats followed by Junior Choir under the movement rule?
options: No, there are only fifteen minutes between them
Yes, there is a full hour between them
No, Paper Boats is only for adults
questions.explanation: A ends10:00 B starts10:15, less than30min. Age10 eligible, so transition fails.

questions.prompt: What should a Garden Watch participant expect?
questions.explanation: D explicitly includes outdoor observation with teacher. Indoor-only/singing not description.
